Q1: Safrole's hazard profile indicates internationally recognized significant concerns (Tier 1) for carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, reproductive hazards (CMR), oral hazards (ORL), and organ/systemic hazards (OGN). It also shows an expanded perspective of potential dermal and eye hazards (Tier 2). However, data is currently deficient (Tier 4) for both acute/chronic environmental hazards (ENV) and inhalation hazards (IHL), while endocrine disruption hazards (EDC) are considered to be of low to moderate concern (Tier 3).
Q2: Safrole is listed on several "Lists of Concern," prominently including California's Proposition 65 and the IARC Carcinogens Group 2B, classifying it as "possibly carcinogenic to humans." It also appears on the "Substitute In Now" list, identifying it as a hazardous chemical recommended for replacement. Interestingly, it is also found on the FDA's "Substances added to Food" list, suggesting its use in highly regulated, very low quantities despite its recognized hazards.
Q3: Safrole is relatively well-characterized, possessing a specific molecular formula (C10H10O2) and being classified as a "Small Molecule," indicating a well-defined structure. It has been extensively studied, with 3,924 literature references—significantly more than the median for chemicals in our fracking and petrochemical dataset. Despite this, its hazard profile still has some data deficiencies, specifically for environmental and inhalation hazards, as indicated by two Tier 4 classifications.
